articles.title: Brasileira ganha prêmio de pizza mais criativa do mundo em Olimpíada | G1
articles.standfirst: A capixaba Carla Dall’Orto Carvalho conquistou troféu em competição realizada em Nápoles. Ela foi a única brasileira a ser premiada no evento.
articles.summary: A capixaba Carla Dall’Orto Carvalho conquistou troféu em competição realizada em Nápoles. Ela foi a única brasileira a ser premiada no evento.
articles.body:
A junção de alguns ingredientes frescos na receita que surgiu a partir de uma compra errada foi a responsável por dar à capixaba Carla Dall’Orto Carvalho, de 44 anos, o prêmio internacional de pizza mais criativa na Olimpíada da Pizza , realizada em Nápoles, na Itália.

A pizzaiola concorreu com mais de 350 participantes de 30 países e foi a única brasileira a ser premiada com a pizza chamada "La Vincitrice", que em italiano significa "a vencedora". O primeiro lugar conquistado foi na categoria "Orto Creativo", que significa "Horta Criativa".

Carla já tinha sido eleita, em 2025, a primeira mulher a vencer uma competição como melhor pizzaiola do Brasil. Conquista que garantiu a ela uma vaga na competição mundial realizada agora em setembro em Nápoles.

A disputa na Itália é conhecida como a maior premiação da Vera Pizza Napoletana Champion. A especialidade, inclusive, é considerada Patrimônio Imaterial da Humanidade pela Unesco.

A pizzaiola capixaba, que começou a trabalhar em uma pizzaria de Vila Velha , na Grande Vitória, em 2022, como lavadora de pratos, disse que ainda não acredita na conquista.

"Nossa! É surreal, né? Ver de onde eu vim, com pouco tempo, viver tudo isso, trazer essa alegria para o Brasil e para as pessoas no Espírito Santo é muito gratificante. Sério, eu ainda não sei o tamanho da dimensão disso tudo ainda", comentou Carla.

Capixaba Carla Dall’Orto Carvalho ganhou prêmio de pizza mais criativa do mundo em Olimpíada na Itália — Foto: TV Gazeta

A receita que trouxe o troféu para terras capixabas veio quando a pizzaiola cometeu um erro na hora de montar a lista de ingredientes que deveria comprar para a pizzaria onde trabalha.

"Era para ter comprado cinco tomates, porque até então, naquela época, a gente só fazia uma salada caprese. Eu botei o zero no lugar errado e chegou 50 tomates aqui. Eu fiquei desesperada! Chegou uma caixa de feira, com dez quilos de tomate. Minha patroa falou: 'Calma, respira'. Eu já tava desesperada. Aí, fomos fazer tomate seco, porque era mês de junho e a gente ia criar um menu para o dia dos namorados", relatou.

Naquele mesmo mês, a pizzaiola participou da etapa brasileira do Vera Pizza Napoletana Champion e ganhou com a melhor técnica de fazer uma pizza de sabor marguerita.

Pizzaiola Carla Dall’Orto Carvalho, 44 anos, ganhou prêmio internacional de pizza mais criativa na Olimpíada da Pizza, na Itália — Foto: Reprodução/TV Gazeta

Ao voltar do campeonato, realizado em São Paulo, ela recebeu a missão de criar um sabor de pizza para celebrar a conquista. Carla não pensou duas vezes: era hora de utilizar os tomates que sobraram. E foi assim que surgiu 'La Vincitrice'.

A pizza passou a fazer parte do cardápio em junho do ano passado e já era uma das mais pedidas do restaurante que fica no bairro Prainha. Após o prêmio internacional, muita gente vai até o local só para pedir a delícia premiada.

"A gente já gosta do restaurante, mas agora viemos prestigiar porque acho que é um trabalho que precisa ser valorizado no estado. A qualidade dos ingredientes, você sente em cada garfada, cada mordida", disse a cliente Adriana Freire.

A mistura de sabores foi o diferencial para que o sabor ficasse em primeiro lugar. Grande parte dos ingredientes são do Espírito Santo, como o queijo muçarela feito por produtores de Alegre, no Sul do estado, e também o manjericão, colhido em Santa Leopoldina, na Região Serrana.

A categoria que Carla ganhou avalia e premia a criatividade culinária, o domínio técnico e a conexão harmônica da receita com o que vem da terra — celebrando o frescor de verduras, ervas e hortaliças da estação em alinhamento com conceitos de cultivo de proximidade (quilômetro zero).

Já com dois prêmios diferentes na mão, a pizzaiola sonha em poder ensinar a prática que hoje faz parte da sua rotina. Em um dia movimentado no restaurante, ela chega a fazer cerca de 200 pizzas, que ficam prontas em aproximadamente de três a quatro minutos.

"Eu tenho uma grande vontade de ensinar as pessoas, poder replicar o que eu aprendi. Assim como fez bem para mim, consegui um emprego, cresci profissionalmente, eu acredito que eu posso ajudar de alguma forma outras mulheres, ou incentivar as pessoas a ter um novo emprego. Só quero transmitir o meu conhecimento", destacou.

O concurso Vera Pizza Napoletana Champion é um campeonato internacional que reúne alguns dos melhores pizzaiolos do mundo para celebrar e premiar a verdadeira pizza napolitana.

O evento é organizado pela AVPN (Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana ou Associação da Verdadeira Pizza Napolitana), entidade oficial sediada na Itália que protege e regulamenta a tradição desse prato no mundo todo.

São três dias de desafios, encontros e debates com a participação de profissionais e entusiastas do mundo.

Os competidores disputam em várias categorias que analisam a forma de fazer os sabores mais tradicionais da pizza.

A conquista da capixaba foi em um prêmio especial dentro da categoria gourmet que mostra um reconhecimento concedido a um pizzaiolo por uma receita onde a horta e a imaginação se fundem e trazem uma inovação no sabor.

Capixaba Carla Dall’Orto Carvalho ganhou prêmio de pizza mais criativa do mundo em Olimpíada na Itália — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Monday denied offering Iran any concessions, after a report emerged that Washington was willing to provide sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds as part of a final agreement if Tehran makes “concrete progress” on the nuclear issue.“I offered them NOTHING!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social, rejecting the claim that his administration had offered Iran sanctions relief.He wrote, "Axios just released a story that “Trump” offered Sanctions Relief and Frozen Funds to Iran. articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan donated $4 million to save a 600-year-old Hawaii fishpond; they won't own the land; nonprofit that now owns says: We plan to restore it as a working...
articles.summary: Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have helped preserve a historic fishpond in Hawaii.
articles.body: Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have helped preserve a historic fishpond in Hawaii. The couple has committed $4 million to ensure the future of Alakoko Fishpond, a roughly 600-year-old aquaculture site on Kauaʻi that had been experiencing environmental degradation and pressure from potential development. That donation helped the Trust for Public Land buy the 102-acre property in 2021 and turn it over to local nonprofit Mālama Hulē‘ia for long-term stewardship. Importantly, Zuckerberg and Chan don’t own the land. Instead, the property is protected as a conservation site.According to a report by Resonate Voices, the nonprofit that now owns the property has plans to restore it as a working fishpond and outdoor classroom where students and volunteers can learn traditional Hawaiian aquaculture, native ecosystems, history and culture. The site, also known as Alekoko or Menehune Fishpond, includes a 2,700-foot-long kuapā, or fishpond wall, and is the largest remaining fishpond on Kauaʻi. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1973 and was named one of Hawaiʻi’s most endangered historic places in 2009.How Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan helped save the fishpondThe effort to protect Alakoko began before Zuckerberg and Chan's donation. Community group Mālama Hulē‘ia had already spent four years restoring the fishpond when its owner decided to sell the property in early 2021. The group feared the historic site could eventually be lost to commercial development.The Trust for Public Land negotiated the purchase and sought private funding to close the gap. Zuckerberg and Chan provided the full US$4 million through the Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi Community Fund of the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation.The funding covered the purchase price and transaction costs and also supported the missions of the Trust for Public Land and Mālama Hulē‘ia. The Trust for Public Land completed the acquisition on November 17, 2021, and transferred the property to Mālama Hulē‘ia for long-term stewardship.Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan do not own the landAlthough they provided the money needed to secure the property, Zuckerberg and Chan do not own any part of Alakoko Fishpond. The land is instead protected for conservation, education and community use in perpetuity, preventing it from being sold to the highest bidder in the future.The arrangement allows Mālama Hulē‘ia to continue its restoration work while keeping the historic site accessible for community activities and education.Plans to restore Alakoko as a working fishpondMālama Hulē‘ia plans to restore the fishpond, surrounding wetlands and estuary. Its long-term goal includes bringing back fish and seafood harvesting while using the site to teach visitors about traditional Hawaiian aquaculture, native ecosystems, history and culture.The project also reflects Chan and Zuckerberg's broader philanthropic activity in Hawaii. Through the Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi Community Fund, the couple has supported local health, education and environmental initiatives, including funding for Wilcox Medical Center and a multi-year commitment to the Hawaiʻi Institute of Marine Biology.The Alakoko project gives the historic fishpond a future as both a working aquaculture site and a place where future generations can learn about Native Hawaiian traditions.You use AI every day. articles.body: The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to an early listing of a plea challenging the manner in which the Election Commission of India (ECI) is functioning, with allegations that powers vested in the multi-member constitutional body are being exercised without adhering to the legally mandated collective decision-making process.Senior advocate Vikas Singh mentioned the matter before a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, arguing that the statutory framework requires decisions of the multi-member Commission to be taken unanimously or by majority.The plea comes amid controversy over ECINet, the ECI’s integrated digital platform for electoral processes. The Indian Express reported concerns raised by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi over the centralisation of electoral-roll databases and access available to state-level officials.The ECI has maintained that ECINet is decentralised and that statutory responsibilities remain with designated election officials.On September 26, the poll panel also formed a committee, headed by a Senior Deputy Election Commissioner and including an independent IIT or IIIT expert, to review ECINet’s compliance with laws and rules.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Pokimane’s latest livestream took an unexpectedly painful turn after the Twitch star shared the heartbreaking news that her beloved cat, Mimi, had died. The eight-year-old pet was taken to an emergency room after reportedly falling from a balcony at Pokimane’s home. What began as a sudden interruption to her Valorant stream quickly became a devastating personal moment, as the streamer struggled to process the loss of a pet who had been part of her life for years.Pokimane reveals what happened to MimiPokimane, whose real name is Imane, abruptly ended her Valorant livestream on September 28 after learning that Mimi had been taken to an emergency room. She later returned to Twitch and explained what had happened.According to Pokimane, cleaners had opened a balcony at her home. Mimi went outside and then jumped from the balcony. Pokimane said she had been streaming at the time and was unaware of what was happening until her sister contacted her."Basically... the emergency was that... my sister told me that they took Mimi to the ER, and I was really confused because I had been streaming the whole time. I was here the whole time, and she jumped."She then described arriving at the emergency room and realising that the situation was more serious than she had initially understood."And... Sorry, I'm a little... (The streamer starts crying) actually, a little in shock. So... also, Chris is here, sorry. I can't believe my baby is gone. I don't know what to say, but you guys have seen Mimi with me since I got her. I'm just so... sad. Everything around me is Mimi. It was my baby."Pokimane pays tribute to her cat MimiPokimane later addressed Mimi’s death on X, telling followers that she had received the devastating news after leaving her stream."sorry for leaving stream abruptly, i was notified my cat was in the ER, and as soon as i made it to the vet they told me she didn’t make it. i love you forever mimi."The post prompted an outpouring of support from fans and fellow creators. Valkyrae also responded to the announcement, writing, "Noooo I’m so sorry Imane.. rest in peace Mimi"Mimi had been with Pokimane for eight years, making the loss especially difficult for the streamer. articles.title: In 1997, two young scientists bought 116 acres beside New Hampshire’s Bear Brook State Park; 25 years later, they placed the entire farm under conservation protection for wetlands, forests and wildlife
articles.summary: Laura Bonk and Phil Trowbridge bought 116 acres of undeveloped land in Allenstown, New Hampshire, in 1997.
articles.body: Laura Bonk and Phil Trowbridge bought 116 acres of undeveloped land in Allenstown, New Hampshire, in 1997. The couple were young scientists and outdoor enthusiasts at the time. They recognised the importance of the property, which lies along the northern boundary of Bear Brook State Park. About 25 years later, they placed the entire property under permanent conservation protection to preserve its wetlands, forests, water resources and wildlife habitat.The land, known as Derevya Farms, forms part of the Merrimack River watershed, according to Society for the Protection of New Hampshire Forests. Its location and natural features make it important for protecting water quality and providing habitat for wildlife. The property also includes frontage along Little Bear Brook, which flows into Bear Brook and the Suncook River. These waterways are tributaries of the Merrimack River watershed.The Bonk-Trowbridge family donated a conservation easement on the property to ensure that its conservation value would be protected permanently. However, the donation did not transfer ownership of the land. The family continues to own the property while its conservation easement protects the land's natural features.The Society for the Protection of New Hampshire Forests helped raise funds to cover the costs of the project and the long-term care of the protected land. The Merrimack Conservation Partnership awarded the project an $8,000 grant because of the property's importance to the watershed. Individual donors from across the state provided the remaining funding.Why the 116-acre property mattersBonk and Trowbridge had planned to conserve the property since they bought it. Their decision came after years of owning and maintaining the land, which has also become a place for local residents to enjoy outdoor recreation.“Ever since we bought the land, we have been planning to conserve it,” Bonk said. Trowbridge said the decision also reflected their priorities at this stage of their lives. “We have reached a stage in life where you need to focus on doing important things. This donation is one of those things,” he said.The property is part of a wider effort to protect the Merrimack River watershed. Over the past decade, conservation, advocacy and educational groups have worked together to preserve important areas across the watershed. The Forest Society and its partners have helped conserve a chain of properties, with Derevya Farms serving as one of the links.The Merrimack River watershed is important for drinking water. According to Jack Savage, president of the Society for the Protection of New Hampshire Forests, more than 700,000 people in Massachusetts and New Hampshire depend on the Merrimack River as a source of drinking water. Groundwater from the watershed also supplies private wells throughout the region.“More than 700,000 people in Massachusetts and New Hampshire rely on the Merrimack River as the source of their drinking water and its groundwater feeds private wells throughout, so the health of the watershed has a direct impact on the quality of the water we drink,” Savage said. He also thanked Bonk and Trowbridge for their contribution and their commitment to protecting the land.Forests and wetlands provide wildlife habitatApart from its role in the watershed, Derevya Farms supports several wildlife species. The property provides habitat for moose, deer, bobcats, migratory birds and other wildlife.Its position beside Bear Brook State Park also makes it important as a route through which animals can move across the landscape. Trowbridge said the couple had long recognised that the property could serve as a travel corridor for wildlife living in the state park.The land has also become a familiar outdoor space for people living nearby. The family maintains trails and a Class VI road through the property, allowing neighbours and local residents to walk through the woods. Trowbridge said the use of these trails had increased over time.“We always knew that Derevya Farms would be a travel corridor for wildlife in Bear Brook State Park. It has also become a travel corridor for people,” Trowbridge said.He added that his neighbours knew the woods and trails as well as he did. Seeing other people use and care for the land had been a rewarding experience, he said. “I am proud to be conserving this open space for everyone to enjoy,” Trowbridge said.Bonk also shared a personal connection to the property. Among her favourite features were the trilliums, a group of wildflowers found on the land. “For me,” Bonk said, “my favorite thing about the land are the trilliums. I love seeing the wildflowers.”Protection intended to last permanentlyThe conservation easement on Derevya Farms is intended to protect the property's conservation values permanently. Such easements allow landowners to retain ownership while placing lasting protections on land with important natural, scenic, water or wildlife resources.The Society for the Protection of New Hampshire Forests said it makes a long-term commitment to every property covered by a conservation easement it accepts. The organisation has used these agreements since the early 1970s to protect more than 130,000 acres of forest land, water resources, scenic views, wildlife habitat and agricultural resources.You use AI every day. articles.title: How a $25,000 beach cottage in Cape Cod became one of the most iconic homes in American history and saw some of its darkest moments
articles.summary: Homes are often more than just four walls and a roof.
articles.body: Homes are often more than just four walls and a roof. They hold memories and tales of the lives lived inside them and are privy to some of the highest and lowest moments of them. One such home is a $25000 beach cottage in Cape Cod that has seen and withstood some of the best and worst moments of American history.The Kennedy Compound is as famous as the family who owns it. Located in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, the property, which is made up of three houses set along the beach of Cape Cod has been the site of numerous moments of American political dynasty. It was where John F. Kennedy brought Jackie after proposing marriage, it functioned as a "summer white house," and it was here that the president's mother Rose, heard of her son's assassination.The fated houseAccording to the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Port Museum, the origins of the Kennedy Compound on Cape Cod can be traced back to 1926. That summer, Kennedy family patriarch Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. rented Malcolm Cottage in Hyannis Port for his family. He had previously tried to find a summer home in Cohasset, a coastal town about an hour from Hyannis Port. However, he was turned down by the exclusive Cohasset Golf Club, allegedly because he was Irish Catholic as per a report by All Things Interesting. When Kennedy Sr. learned that Hyannisport Club was more welcoming to Irish Catholics, he decided to give it a try.He liked the area immensely and purchased Malcolm Cottage two years later for $25,000. This is the house that soon became known as the Kennedy Compound. It became the summer destination for the Kennedy clan which at the time included Joseph, his wife Rose, and their children: Joseph Jr., John, Rosemary, Kathleen, Eunice, Patricia, Robert, Jean, and Edward.As an adult, John F. Kennedy bought his own home in Hyannis Port, just behind his father's house. So did his younger brother, Robert. These three oceanside properties, which total six acres, make up what's known today as the Kennedy Compound.A history of lives well-livedJohn F. Kennedy spent many happy days in Hyannis Port. As he geared up to run for president in 1960, the Kennedy Compound became the headquarters of his presidential campaign. He even watched the election results here after voting in Boston, and it was here that he celebrated his victory over Richard Nixon. Though his presidency took JFK to Washington, D.C., he and his family still spent their summers at the Kennedy Compound, which came to be known as the "Summer White House.""Hyannis Port became, during the summers, a major national and international dateline," the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Port Museum explains. "The massive and intensive press coverage — newspapers, TV and glossy magazine colour photos — of the wealthy, powerful and glamorous family at work and play in seaside settings focused national attention on Cape Cod."But on November 22, 1963, the Kennedy White House became tinged with news that would change the lives of the family forever. Rose Kennedy was at home when her son Robert, then the attorney general, called her to let her know that JFK had been shot in Dallas. Later, he called again to let her know that the President was dead. The assassination of John F. Kennedy marked the end of an era. But the Kennedy Compound remained an important meeting place for his family.A generational homeThe Kennedy family continued to spend time in Hyannis Port in the second half of the 20th century. In 1994, 30 years after the president's assassination, his son, John F. Kennedy Jr., brought his then-girlfriend, Carolyn Bessette, to the Kennedy Compound to meet his famous family. According to 'The Kennedy Heirs: John, Caroline, and the New Generation — A Legacy of Tragedy and Triumph' by J. Randy Taraborrelli, the meeting did not go well. JFK Jr.'s aunt Ethel (the wife of Robert Kennedy, who had been assassinated in 1968) quizzed guests on current events. Ethel asked Carolyn about the federal assault weapons ban, and when Carolyn expressed ignorance, Ethel remarked: "You may want to read up on it."Though Bessette purportedly swore she would never return to the Kennedy Compound, she did. She and JFK Jr., then her husband, were flying to Hyannis Port to attend a family wedding when their plane crashed off the coast of Martha's Vineyard on July 16, 1999, killing the couple and Bessette's sister, Lauren.Indeed, Hyannis Port was often the site of sad events. Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. died there in 1969; so did his wife, Rose, in 1995, and their son, Ted Kennedy, in 2009. But the family has also celebrated many happy occasions at the Kennedy Compound, from the engagement of JFK and Jackie back in 1953 to the marriage of Robert and Ethel's granddaughter, Sarah Kennedy, in 2023.Now, roughly a century since the house was first bought, the Kennedy family still spends their summers at the home. In recent years, the entire family has gathered to celebrate the Fourth of July together in Hyannis Port. In that way, the Kennedy Compound is still an important place. Not only is it special to the Kennedy family to this day, but the sweeping grounds of the compound, with its views of Nantucket Sound, are also imbued with history."Don't let it be forgot, that once there was a spot, for one brief shining moment that was known as Camelot, and it will never be that way again," said Jackie Kennedy famously to a Life reporter from the Kennedy Compound just four days after her husband's funeral and this house is just that.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Florida teen sentenced to 50 years in prison after pleading guilty to killing mother and her boyfriend in planned ambush
articles.summary: Florida teenager Julia Grace Egler, 18, has been sentenced to 50 years in state prison after pleading guilty to killing her mother and her mother’s
articles.body: Florida teenager Julia Grace Egler, 18, has been sentenced to 50 years in state prison after pleading guilty to killing her mother and her mother’s boyfriend in Palm Bay in July 2024. Egler was 16 when Kelley McCollom and Matthew Szejnrok were killed. Prosecutors said she had planned the attack, staged a fake home invasion and waited for the couple to return before shooting them. According to investigators, Egler greeted the couple by saying “Welcome home” before opening fire. She later pleaded guilty to two counts of second-degree murder under a negotiated agreement that reduced the original first-degree murder charges. At her September 25, 2026, sentencing, a judge imposed a 50-year prison term, with a mandatory minimum of 25 years before she can seek sentence review, followed by 20 years of supervised probation.How the Florida teen planned the ambush on her mother and boyfriendThe killings occurred shortly after midnight on July 7, 2024, at McCollom’s home in Palm Bay, Florida. According to the Palm Bay Police investigation, Egler initially contacted 911 and reported that an unknown person had broken into the house.Officers responding to the call found McCollom dead in the living room from gunshot wounds. Szejnrok was found dead in a bathroom with gunshot and stab wounds.Investigators subsequently determined that the evidence did not support Egler’s account of an outside intruder. Police said there was no convincing evidence of forced entry and that other evidence at the scene pointed to someone inside the home.According to the investigation, Egler later admitted that she had staged the burglary. Police said she had taken a .38-calibre revolver and ammunition from her mother’s bedroom and waited for McCollom and Szejnrok to return.What happened when the couple came homeInvestigators said Egler was waiting inside the home when McCollom and Szejnrok arrived. According to the arrest affidavit, she greeted them by saying “Welcome home” before opening fire.Police said Egler shot both victims with the revolver. After she ran out of ammunition, investigators alleged that she picked up a kitchen knife and stabbed Szejnrok.The account formed part of the evidence used by prosecutors in the case. Egler was subsequently arrested and prosecuted as an adult.The investigation also found that the alleged attack had been preceded by conflict within the household, although prosecutors ultimately resolved the case through a negotiated guilty plea rather than a trial on the original charges.What investigators said about the motiveAccording to Palm Bay police and prosecutors, tensions within the family were among the circumstances examined during the investigation. Authorities said Egler was unhappy about her mother’s relationship with Szejnrok.Investigators also said there had been conflict surrounding Egler’s gender transition and her mother’s response to it. These issues were cited by authorities as part of the background to the case.Szejnrok was 22 when he was killed. Prosecutors alleged that the disagreements contributed to the circumstances surrounding the attack, but the case was ultimately resolved through a plea agreement rather than a jury determination of the precise motive.Why the charges were reducedEgler was initially charged with two counts of first-degree premeditated murder following the killings. Because she was 16 when the offences occurred, her case involved Florida's rules governing juveniles who are prosecuted as adults.In September 2026, Egler pleaded guilty to two counts of second-degree murder as part of a negotiated agreement with prosecutors.The State Attorney’s Office said the agreement was approved by surviving family members. It brought the case to a conclusion without requiring the victims’ relatives to go through a jury trial and the presentation of evidence in open court.The plea also meant that Egler was sentenced on the amended second-degree murder charges rather than facing trial on the original first-degree charges.How long will Julia Egler remain in prisonCircuit Judge Michelle Naberhaus sentenced Egler to 50 years in Florida state prison on September 25, 2026.Because Egler was 16 when the murders occurred, the sentence includes provisions concerning when she can seek a review of her sentence. According to the State Attorney’s Office, she must serve a mandatory minimum of 25 years before becoming eligible for sentence review.After completing her prison term, Egler is required to undergo a mental-health evaluation and serve 20 years of supervised probation.The sentence therefore extends well beyond her teenage years and into adulthood, while the sentence-review provision reflects her age at the time of the crimes.What Egler said at sentencingDuring the sentencing hearing, Egler apologised and asked the court for an opportunity to eventually return to society.Her guilty plea brought the criminal proceedings to an end without a trial. The victims’ relatives were also given an opportunity to address the court through victim-impact statements.The State Attorney’s Office said the plea agreement provided a resolution for the families while avoiding the additional emotional strain of a murder trial.What the victims’ families saidSzejnrok’s brother, Dustin, delivered a victim-impact statement during the sentencing hearing. He described the continuing impact of his brother’s death on the family.The State Attorney’s Office said relatives were still dealing with the consequences of the killings, including the fact that family members continued to live next to the property where the murders occurred.The plea agreement allowed the families to receive a sentence without having to testify through a full trial on the original first-degree murder charges.What the case means for Egler’s futureEgler was 16 when the killings occurred and 18 when she received her sentence. Her case illustrates how a serious offence committed by a juvenile can proceed through Florida’s adult criminal justice system while still taking the defendant’s age at the time of the crime into account at sentencing.Her 50-year sentence, the 25-year mandatory minimum and the subsequent 20 years of supervised probation were imposed after she admitted responsibility for the two killings through her guilty plea.With the September 25 sentencing, the prosecution arising from the 2024 deaths of Kelley McCollom and Matthew Szejnrok has now concluded.You use AI every day. articles.title: Confession can't be sole ground to convict a person under NSA: SC fines UP govt Rs 10 lakh
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday imposed a cost of Rs 10 lakh on the Uttar Pradesh government, holding that a confession statement by an accused
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday imposed a cost of Rs 10 lakh on the Uttar Pradesh government, holding that a confession statement by an accused cannot, by itself, form the basis for his detention under the National Security Act (NSA).Uttar Pradesh Police had invoked the NSA against Mulla Afroz in October 2025 over his alleged involvement in the 2024 communal violence in Sambhal.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu delivered the judgment while quashing Afroz’s preventive detention.The NSA empowers the Centre and state governments to detain individuals to prevent them from acting in a manner deemed “prejudicial to the defence of India”. Detention can be ordered for up to 12 months, although it can be revoked earlier.Tensions escalated in Sambhal in November 2024 during a court-ordered survey of the Shahi Jama Masjid, following claims that a Harihar temple had previously stood at the site.On November 24, during the second round of the survey, protesters clashed with security personnel. The violence left four people dead and dozens injured.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1939, a Superman comic was tucked away in a family attic; eight decades later, three brothers found it and it sold for a record $9.12 million
articles.summary: A long-lost copy of Superman No. 1, hidden in an attic for eight decades, sold for an astonishing $9.12 million at auction, breaking previous records and highlighting the enduring legacy of the iconic superhero.
articles.body: An original copy of Superman No. 1 is commanding the spotlight by realizing $9.12 million on the block according to Heritage Auctions. The coveted pop culture artifact was first printed by DC Comics in the summer of 1939 and remained sequestered away in an unpaved attic in San Francisco waiting to be found. Three unnamed brothers in their 50s and 60s while sorting through their late mother’s residential belongings found the collectible inside a plain cardboard box.According to auction house profiles, the box was replete with an unknown family trove of vintage golden-age comics that the brother’s uncle bought during the Great Depression through World War II. Lon Allen, Vice President at Heritage Auctions revealed that there were only rumours surrounding the collection but the family had never actually seen the physical copies. The identity of the final winning bidder who secured the issue has not been divulged to the public.The industry’s metric system of grading Before landing in the auction block, the comic book was sent for professional authentication and preservation review to the Certified Guaranty Company (CGC). Even though it spent decades in cardboard under a pile of decaying newspapers, the condition of the comic remained immaculate. The comic registered a rare 9.0 out of the 10-point metric system used in the industry, a score that is reserved only for copies with bright inks, tight spines, and exceptional preservation. In doing so, it became the highest-graded copy of Superman No. 1 in the CGC Population Report, surpassing the previous auction record set by the Mile High pedigree copy (graded CGC 8.0), which sold privately for $5.3 million in 2022.When DC Comics first introduced the issue in 1939, it sold out an initial print run of 500,000 copies. To accommodate surging newsstand demand, the company followed up with secondary runs of 250,000 and then 150,000 copies. Despite roughly 900,000 copies making it to circulation, finding intact specimens remains exceptionally rare. The main reason why so many copies were damaged is that the original cover had a printed marketing invitation urging kids to cut it off and hang it up as a bedroom poster. As of today, only 209 total copies of Superman No. 1 are recorded in the global CGC registry and less than half of its specimens have managed to maintain the highly desired blue Universal label.Tracing its history and place in the pop culture The comic’s cultural weight is part of what drove the bidding. Conceived by two Cleveland teenagers, Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, Superman was created in 1938. Now it is regarded as a foundational comic book, and part of a specialized tier known as "big three," which includes Action Comics No. 1 and Detective Comics No. 27. While Superman as a character made its debut in 1938 as an ensemble feature within the pages of Action Comics No. 1, the 1939 Superman No. 1 was the first issue of an ongoing series that ran 423 issues over the next 47 years, ending in 1986, according to library holdings records. Moreover, it marked the first time in global publishing history for a fictional comic protagonist to receive a standalone title entirely dedicated to their own adventures.The visual layout of the comic book boldly presents the Man of Steel on its cover touting "64 pages of action" printed "all in full color" to its readers. The landmark sale accentuates a staggering financial departure when compared to the character’s humble commercial beginnings. When teenage creators Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster first brought the character to market, they signed away its intellectual property rights to DC Comics for a modest $130 check, a sum too little when considering the household name it would go on to establish.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Wisconsin family will keep owning and logging nearly 1,800 forest acres while a $1.6 million deal permanently blocks development and opens almost 1,500 acres to hikers, hunters and anglers
articles.summary: A Wisconsin family will continue to own and manage nearly 1,800 acres of forest in Langlade County after the state moved closer to securing a $1.6 million
articles.body: A Wisconsin family will continue to own and manage nearly 1,800 acres of forest in Langlade County after the state moved closer to securing a $1.6 million conservation easement on the property. The agreement would prevent the land from being developed while allowing timber production to continue. It would also open almost 1,500 acres to public activities including hiking, hunting and fishing.According to Wisconsin Public Radio, the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (DNR) is seeking the easement from Braun Woodlands II, LLC and the Frederic H.T. Braun Grandchildren Irrevocable Trust. The state’s Natural Resources Board approved the DNR’s request to purchase the easement on Wednesday. The deal would be funded through a combination of state and federal money, along with a planned contribution from the Ice Age Trail Alliance.The proposed protection comes as the forest faces pressure from nearby development. Ron Gropp, the DNR’s forest legacy programme coordinator, said the property could otherwise be broken up as development spreads around it. He said the Braun family decided that protecting the land was the right step for the property’s future.“I think they just came to the conclusion on their own terms that now is the right time to protect this property,” Gropp told the board. “They see the threat going all around them, and they just really feel deeply about this property being protected,” he added.The land covers two separate tracts that will remain in the Braun family’s ownership and stay on the tax rolls. The forest includes northern mixed hardwood, forested wetlands and meadows. Under the proposed easement, almost 1,500 acres would be available to the public, while the remaining part would stay closed to public access and would not be paid for using Stewardship funding.$1.6 million conservation easementThe DNR would pay $1.6 million for the conservation easement. Nearly $1.3 million of that amount would come from a combination of a federal grant and Wisconsin’s Warren Knowles-Gaylord Nelson Stewardship Programme.The Stewardship Programme expired in June after lawmakers did not reauthorise its funding. However, the DNR said money for this particular project had already been restricted under a purchase contract before the programme ended.The final funding arrangement still depends on approval of a federal Forest Legacy grant from the US Forest Service. Gropp said the DNR is not expected to know the status of that grant until early next year. The agency said there is nevertheless enough Stewardship funding available to finance the full purchase.The proposed conservation easement would also protect more than one mile of the existing Ice Age National Scenic Trail. The Ice Age Trail Alliance plans to add another two miles of trail on the property in an area where there is currently no path.Kevin Thusius, the alliance’s senior director of field operations, said the arrangement would allow the Braun family to continue its timber management while protecting part of the trail.“They get this great opportunity to leave a legacy of timber management, and we get to protect the Ice Age National Scenic Trail. The state and other parties get to also have this continued income of timber production,” Thusius told WPR. The alliance plans to contribute around $330,000 towards the purchase, subject to approval by its board.Forest will remain in family ownershipThe conservation deal does not involve the state taking ownership of the entire property. Instead, the easement would place permanent limits on development while the Braun family continues to own the land.The property has also long been enrolled in Wisconsin’s Managed Forest Law programme. The programme lowers property taxes for private landowners who take part in sustainable forest management.As part of the proposed arrangement, the Braun family has agreed to open 220 acres currently in the Managed Forest Law programme. In return, 320 acres on the western side of the property would be closed to the public.Gropp also pointed to the connection between the forest and the local timber industry. Wood products from the property have gone directly to White Lake, where a Robbins Sports Surfaces manufacturing plant operates.“So really, really impressive that wood from this property goes directly to support that local business and the local economy,” Gropp said.The forest is also located within half a mile of a concentrated animal feeding operation, according to the DNR. Gropp said the surrounding development pressure was one of the reasons protecting the property was important.Public access and Ice Age TrailAlong with keeping the forest under private ownership, the proposed easement would provide public access to almost 1,500 acres. People would be able to use the land for hiking, hunting and fishing.The Ice Age Trail is another major part of the project. More than a mile of existing trail would be protected through the easement, while the Ice Age Trail Alliance plans to build another two miles on the property.Several local and regional bodies have supported the proposed conservation easement. The towns of Evergreen and Polar, the Langlade County Board of Supervisors and the Menominee Indian Tribe have all passed resolutions supporting the establishment of the Braun Woodlands Forest Legacy Conservation Easement.You use AI every day. articles.title: Can Gen Z be swayed by ‘FOMO’, ‘MIA’ or ‘delulu’?
articles.summary: Hello and welcome to the 101st edition of The Weekly Vine.
articles.body: Hello and welcome to the 101st edition of The Weekly Vine. A hundred editions is a long time for one format, and now, to paraphrase the great American songwriter Robert Allen Zimmerman, it’s time for a little change. Instead of whining, sorry, Vining, about five different topics, we are going to focus on one topic and one topic only.People keep asking me what I think of the student protests. They probably wouldn’t if they knew that when I was in Class I, I copied my mother’s signature in the school diary in protest against the authoritarian, Big Brotherly tendencies of teachers. Instead of acknowledging my right to privacy, the school almost expelled me. My only regret till now is that I wasn’t proficient enough at cursive writing to get away with it.Anyway, back to the question: why do folks ask me what I think? Because they have been hoodwinked by the Macaulay-Higgins Complex, a term yours truly created that Google’s AI mode confidently describes as the “post-colonial tendency to treat people who speak and write English fluently as intellectually, socially and morally superior”. And perhaps people keep asking me what I think because I usually answer in Tharoorist English that would have Lord Macaulay’s approval.But jokes apart, all said and done, the recent protests were the first time I felt truly represented in Indian politics.This was a movement led by Gen Z folks who love playing FIFA, can’t survive without air-conditioning, love burgers, delegate fasting to higher-ups, use parliamentary language that could have been lifted from an Anurag Kashyap film and celebrate their victories by dancing. This was much to the chagrin of their opponents and even some of their older allies, who couldn’t understand why their thousand-word edits did not elicit the same response as Instagram reels.It had everything one would want in a popular movie: Bihari protesters demanding equal treatment with their Delhi brethren, including proper tear gas and water cannons; a Salman Khan cameo; a BDSM enthusiast from yesteryear keeping a maun vrat and then realising no one really cared; folks doing fit checks to see whether their outfits were suitable for Jantar Mantar aesthetics; unparliamentary words to describe leaders; and, finally, a concession from the powers that be, who don’t concede.Beneath the carnival, however, lay a fairly straightforward grievance.Indians have a very high tolerance for inequities. We barely complain when potholes swallow us whole. We are fine traversing streets that make Takeshi’s Castle look like a stroll in the park. We breathe poisonous air that would give Darth Vader asthma. We file income tax returns for roads that destroy our cars’ suspension systems, assuming the cars survive ethanol blending.Perhaps this tolerance endured because we always had one escape route, one Stairway to Heaven, to borrow the words of Messrs Plant and Page: competitive examinations.The exam is the great Indian secular faith. Crack it, and all that glitters can be yours. It is one of the few institutions revered almost equally in every kind of household. Families reorganise their entire existence around one child’s preparation. Parents exhaust their savings on coaching institutes. Weddings, festivals and even family illnesses are expected to accommodate the examination calendar.The starting line was never equal. A richer child has private tutors, the privilege of knowing the grammar of the elite, a quiet room, good nutrition and several years of coaching. Yet the central promise endured: someone without those privileges could still make it through time, inclination, intelligence and extraordinary effort.IITian-turned-journalist Sandipan Deb captured the idea in his book The IITians, which described the graduates of independent India’s first great educational institutions as “Midnight’s Brahmins”. The phrase came from Congress leader and fellow IITian Jairam Ramesh, who saw the IITians as a new secular elite created after India’s tryst with destiny, technocrats who replaced scripture with science.The sobriquet was meant for the IITs, but every competitive examination offered a version of the same promise. The right rank could vanquish generations of poverty. It could turn the child of a farmer, shopkeeper or government clerk into the CEO of a multinational company, a chief bureaucrat or a scientist landing a spacecraft on the “dark side of the Moon”. It could transform the prospects of an entire family through the grit of one child’s intellect.Government exams are a purer version of this promise. The salary might be modest, but the job offers respect, security, status and pension, and the hope that the next generation will begin the race a few metres ahead. In vast parts of India, the appointment letter remained the most plausible instrument of social mobility ever invented.Then the dream began springing leaks.The NEET-UG controversy of 2024, the cancellation of UGC-NET and numerous state-level recruitment scandals had already eroded trust. Each cancellation carries the cost of a train ticket, another year without earnings, another loan and the furrowed brows of parents waiting for the future to change. NEET-UG 2026 simply became the straw that broke the camel’s back, the leak epitomising the breakdown of a secret covenant between the student and the Republic.The powers that be responded with a method of communication that had become sui generis and had worked very well since 2014.Question the motivations of the protesters.Search for political forces behind them.Warn that anti-national elements might exploit the agitation.Use force. Turn the grievance into an ideological contest.Remind everyone of the Congress’s failures. Blame Nehru if required.The problem was that this time the old grammar did not fit the subject.Many of the protesters were genuinely non-political, simply angry at a future stolen. They had followed all the rules laid down by the state and were still being shortchanged. There is no ideological manifesto that can be removed, no demand for a revolution. The grievance was immediate, personal, painful and all too real for parents across the country.The other problem that the government faces is generational.Someone who is 21 today was nine when Narendra Modi became Prime Minister. Manmohan Singh, the Commonwealth Games scandal, 26/11, 2G, Anna Hazare and the arguments that propelled the BJP to power belong to a political prehistory they encountered through YouTube clips, WhatsApp forwards and relatives who still become animated whenever someone says “coal allocation”.This generation has never known the BJP as an insurgent force standing outside the establishment. For them, the BJP is the establishment. Congress’s failures are immaterial to them. Telling students “it’s better now” is akin to telling people in the 1960s that life was better post-British rule.Congress’s failures remain historically relevant. They have diminishing value as an answer to a leaked question paper in 2026. The new Gen Z has no memory of Congress rule; it did not live through it. It has grown up in a Digital India of instant payments, biometric identification, online applications and Mann Ki Baat. The system that gave us Digital India cannot suddenly plead administrative helplessness when a national examination collapses like a wave function.A political operation capable of monitoring every opposition remark, producing instant rebuttals and turning speeches into reels within minutes cannot explain that protecting a question paper is simply too complicated. The promise of supreme competence produced expectations of supreme competence.This does not make Gen Z one political species. This author happens to spend a lot of time with Gen Z, listening to their hopes, dreams and aspirations. Its members do not share one ideology, leader or cultural outlook. Many are culturally conservative, strongly nationalist and broadly sympathetic to the BJP. Others are liberal, Left-wing, apolitical or interested only in obtaining the job for which they have spent years preparing. Many prefer Dhurandhar and Rang De Basanti at the same time. Others recognise that they are both propaganda and yet enjoy them for their art.What unites them is a set of common conditions: expensive education, fierce competition, economic anxiety, uncertain employment and a lifetime spent under the same central government.When the familiar communication methods failed, senior Indian politicians attempted something even more ridiculous: speaking the language of Gen Z.The Prime Minister started making reels. Parliamentarians started saying “clocked it”, “MIA”, “FOMO” and “delulu”. Perhaps the finest example of this changing conversation was a gym video in which youngsters discussed the protests through a thicket of catchphrases. One character blamed another for failing to “clock” what India was like when they were ten before urging everyone to build their bodies and the country together. It was what the young folks call cringe.As former Rajya Sabha MP Priyanka Chaturvedi noted: “Gen Z coded. Not.”BJP members and supporters, speaking privately, admitted that the approach was terribly ham-handed. The reel launched a thousand satirical responses, almost all of which were funnier than the original.The problem lay deeper than embarrassing slang. The government had mistaken a crisis of trust for a crisis of communication.Young people may still enjoy propaganda that confirms their beliefs, but they can recognise an uncle reciting internet slang from a briefing note, almost like the 30 Rock scene of Steve Buscemi with a backwards cap asking: “How do you do, fellow kids?”Gen Z’s parents can be scared by the past, but the Gen Z revolution is not televised; it’s on Instagram Reels. It cannot be controlled with narratives. The algorithm is too mutinous and chaotic to control.The movement’s apparent frivolity made it harder for the political class to understand. The dancing, memes, fit checks, references and profanity led older observers to mistake a different aesthetic for a lack of seriousness.It’s just a different medium of protest.Post-colonial scholars often argue that politeness is a symbol of colonial oppression. The lack of solemnity is a similar weapon. Mockery denies the government the battlefield it preferred. A television debate could portray an activist as dangerous, misinformed or politically compromised. A meme, on the other hand, can travel halfway around the globe before the news anchor has tied his shoelaces.Even if Dipke and Co became the face of the cockroach movement, the anger was collective.The opposition should be equally careful about reading the protests as an endorsement, irrespective of bypoll results. A generation with no meaningful memory of Congress in government has very little nostalgia for it. Anger against an incumbent does not automatically become affection for whoever occupies the opposition benches. Every party trying to communicate through borrowed slang risks receiving the same merciless treatment.For more than a decade, the government’s political genius lay in understanding the media environment better than its opponents. It mastered WhatsApp and social media even as its opponents depended on the established media to get their point across. But every successful playbook comes with an expiry date.Students don’t need politicians to speak the lingo of Gen Z. They need an acceptance of their grievances, not ministers posting reels and saying “delulu”. History has shown that student protests, in particular, have a tendency to escape the boundaries initially drawn around them.In 19th-century China, Hong Xiuquan repeatedly failed the imperial civil service examinations, started imagining he was a brother of Jesus and eventually led the Taiping Rebellion, which established a rival state and took the Qing dynasty 15 years to crush at the cost of 20 million lives.India’s experience is less apocalyptic, though no less instructive. Students participated in the movements that challenged British rule. After Independence, the anti-Hindi agitations transformed Tamil Nadu’s political landscape. A protest over hostel food prices in Gujarat helped ignite the Nav Nirman movement. Student unrest in Bihar grew into Jayaprakash Narayan’s call for Sampoorna Kranti, challenged Indira Gandhi and produced a generation of leaders who continue to shape Indian politics.The Mandal protests of 1990 began on campuses, triggered tragic self-immolations and helped reorder the country’s debate over caste, reservations and political representation. These movements shared little ideologically. What they shared was a pattern: a grievance the government considered containable became a vessel for much wider discontent.The Cockroach protests are neither the Taiping Rebellion nor the JP Movement. They might end as a remarkable five-week uprising followed by a ministerial resignation and a few administrative reforms. Yet governments have repeatedly discovered that student anger rarely remains confined to the classroom once it becomes a larger argument about fairness, opportunity and the legitimacy of the system itself.For years, India’s students were told that their futures depended on clearing an examination. This summer, the Cockroaches forced the government to realise that it was being examined too. History is a strict invigilator. It seldom grants re-tests. And those who don’t learn from history are condemned to repeat it.To borrow a line from the only songwriter to have won the Nobel Prize in Literature, “the times they are a-changin’”.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: California thieves steal Nvidia-branded trailers expecting expensive AI hardware; find 40,000 pounds of sand instead
articles.summary: Two Nvidia-branded trailers belonging to autonomous-trucking company PlusAI were stolen from outside its warehouse in Fremont, California, on September
articles.body: Two Nvidia-branded trailers belonging to autonomous-trucking company PlusAI were stolen from outside its warehouse in Fremont, California, on September 23, 2026. The trailers were associated with PlusAI's work with Nvidia on autonomous-driving technology, but instead of carrying GPUs, servers or other expensive AI equipment, each contained about 20,000 pounds of sand. The pair therefore carried roughly 40,000 pounds, or 20 tons, of sand. PlusAI uses the material as simulated cargo during autonomous-truck testing to reproduce the weight of real freight. The trailers were later discovered in nearby Newark after an acquaintance of a PlusAI executive spotted them, while police continued investigating the theft.California thieves found sand inside the Nvidia-branded trailersThe two trailers were parked outside PlusAI's Fremont facility when they were taken overnight. Their locks were broken and the thieves apparently arrived with tractor units, connected them to the trailers and drove away. Both trailers prominently displayed PlusAI and Nvidia branding, reflecting the companies' work in autonomous trucking and artificial intelligence.The company's autonomous-driving truck cabs remained inside the facility and were not stolen. The stolen trailers were later located in Newark, California, roughly half a mile from PlusAI's Fremont warehouse.What was inside the stolen trailersThe trailers contained about 20,000 pounds of sand each, giving them a combined load of approximately 40,000 pounds, or 20 tons. The sand was being used as simulated cargo during PlusAI's testing programme.Heavy simulated cargo allows autonomous-truck developers to reproduce the conditions of a loaded commercial vehicle without using an actual freight shipment. The added weight can be used to test how a truck responds during acceleration, braking, turning and other driving conditions.Why PlusAI uses sand to test autonomous trucksPlusAI develops autonomous-driving technology for commercial trucks, meaning its vehicles must be tested under conditions that resemble real-world freight operations. Vehicle behaviour can change significantly depending on how much weight a truck is carrying.Using sand provides a practical way to create a controlled and consistent load. Engineers can adjust the amount of weight while testing different driving scenarios, helping them study how the autonomous system and vehicle respond when operating under the demands of a loaded truck.How the stolen trailers were foundThe trailers were eventually spotted in Newark, close to PlusAI's Fremont facility. An acquaintance of a PlusAI executive reportedly noticed the trailers and sent a photograph to the executive after recognising them.The company contacted authorities, who located and recovered both trailers. The sand was still inside, allowing PlusAI to recover both the vehicles and their testing cargo.What police said about the theftThe Fremont Police Department investigated the theft after the trailers were reported missing. Security footage reportedly showed two unidentified tractor units near the PlusAI facility around the time of the incident.PlusAI said the tractor units did not belong to the company. Investigators were working to identify the people involved and determine how the trailers were taken from the facility.The connection between PlusAI and NvidiaThe Nvidia branding on the trailers reflected the companies' collaboration in autonomous trucking. PlusAI works with Nvidia on computing and artificial-intelligence technology used in autonomous vehicles.Nvidia's technology is widely used in AI development and autonomous-driving systems, making its branding highly recognisable in the technology industry. However, the trailers themselves were being used by PlusAI for autonomous-truck testing, with the confirmed cargo consisting of sand rather than Nvidia computing equipment.The theft produced an unexpected discovery when two trailers carrying prominent technology-company branding turned out to be loaded with 40,000 pounds of sand. The trailers had been taken from PlusAI's Fremont facility but were found only about half a mile away in Newark.Both trailers and their simulated cargo were recovered, while investigators continued working to identify the people responsible for the theft.You use AI every day. articles.title: The radical thing you should do instead of '80s challenge
articles.summary: The Weekly Vine, Edition 106: The radical thing you should do instead of the ’80s AI photo challenge I tell everyone who is willing to listen that there
articles.body: The Weekly Vine, Edition 106: The radical thing you should do instead of the ’80s AI photo challengeI tell everyone who is willing to listen that there are three great dystopian novels one needs to read. The first, by Bihari lad George Orwell, is obviously Nineteen Eighty-Four. Orwell, born Eric Arthur Blair in Motihari, discovered, much like Buddha before him, that any association with the state condemns one to a lifetime of ennui. The second is Brave New World by Aldous Huxley, which imagines a world where humanity gives in to its pleasures and people become unteachable.I will mention the third at the end of the Vine. Consider it book bait, if you will.The two masters of dystopia have a destiny that seems strangely intertwined because Huxley also happened to teach Orwell French at Eton and would later school him about dystopia, which the French call just existing.In 1949, after Nineteen Eighty-Four was published, Huxley wrote to his former student, praised the book and then, like all teachers, proceeded to explain where the student had gone wrong.Orwell imagined a world where Big Brother was in complete control and ruled through fear, the Thought Police, telescreens and the proverbial boot stamping on a human face. Huxley argued that the ruling oligarchy would find “less arduous and wasteful ways of governing” than beating everyone into submission.Why spend so much effort forcing people to obey, he wondered, when you could make them enjoy obedience? Why ban something people no longer wanted? Why seize information when people might happily volunteer it?Nearly four decades later, American media theorist Neil Postman turned the Huxley-Orwell divide into the central argument of Amusing Ourselves to Death.Postman wrote:“What Orwell feared were those who would ban books. What Huxley feared was that there would be no reason to ban a book, for there would be no one who wanted to read one. Orwell feared those who would deprive us of information. Huxley feared those who would give us so much that we would be reduced to passivity and egoism. Orwell feared that the truth would be concealed from us. Huxley feared the truth would be drowned in a sea of irrelevance. Orwell feared we would become a captive culture. Huxley feared we would become a trivial culture, preoccupied with some equivalent of the feelies, the orgy porgy, and the centrifugal bumblepuppy. As Huxley remarked in Brave New World Revisited, the civil libertarians and rationalists who are ever on the alert to oppose tyranny “failed to take into account man’s almost infinite appetite for distractions.” In 1984, Huxley added, people are controlled by inflicting pain. In Brave New World, they are controlled by inflicting pleasure.”All of which brings us today to the algorithm: the love-child of a not-quite AGI Deus Ex Machina and the Mammon lovers powering it, which goes by many different names. And like a remarkable orchestrator, this algorithm has managed to make the entire populace dance to its tunes without even so much as a threat.The latest iteration is the ’80s challenge, where suddenly everyone is using ChatGPT’s updated image software to post more hirsute, denim-clad versions of themselves as though they were auditioning for a Mithun Chakraborty film, letting nostalgia rob them of the notion that we considered much of this quite cringe back then.It was a simple reminder that when Big Tech asks for our data, we tell it to eff off, but the moment sharing our data is presented as a challenge, we happily jump on the digital bandwagon and share all our information with a cherry on top.It’s hard not to do it.If there was peer pressure in the real world, today the entire digital space is a peer-to-peer sharing group modifying our behaviours, and at this moment the trend has escaped Twitter and LinkedIn to end up with the WhatsApp and Instagram crowd.Freedom, Jean-Paul Sartre argued, is what we do with what’s been done to us. Perhaps Sartre understood what Huxley did too: humans don’t need to be coerced to imitate one another.We have always blindly followed the crazy trends of the day, like lemmings jumping off a cliff. As an aside, lemmings don’t actually commit suicide, and the myth is based partly on a scene from the Disney documentary White Wilderness, in which animals were driven over a cliff into a river.But we have been proverbial lemmings, even when lemmings aren’t proverbial lemmings, long before the algorithm came to control us.French thinker René Girard argued that desire itself is mimetic: what we call keeping up with the Joneses. When we see someone else with something, our heart desires it like Eve’s apple. So many of our desires are based on looking at someone else’s possessions, whether fashion, status, political opinion or even the sudden desire to look like a Disco Dancer extra.The algorithm didn’t invent desire any more than McDonald’s invented hunger, but it learnt how to industrialise it. Before, peer pressure required actual peers.Sometimes those peers were a deterrent too, as one has explained with the Toaster F*** Theory. For those who don’t read closely enough, before the internet, if someone said they wanted to perform coitus with electrical equipment, they were told to shut up or sent to an asylum. Now, you go online and announce your desire and suddenly find 10,000 other people who want to do the same thing, which convinces you that f****** toasters is normative behaviour.Peer pressure works in the same way: you needed to find someone to feel jealous of. The internet removed that geographical limitation and gave us a superset peer group that includes everyone from our childhood friends to complete strangers to celebrities.The question here really isn’t even what Big Tech can make us do, but how much of what we are doing is a choice. If a challenge can make us do these things, what real choices are we making every day? Are we choosing what we want to eat, wear or believe each day? Or, as Huxley pointed out, is coercion not the only enemy?A man being marched at gunpoint knows he’s not free. But is the man who finds happiness on a billboard equally unfree? The first man can at least see his chains; the second perhaps doesn’t recognise that his choices have left him chained.Are we anything more than the sum total of our desires and social conditioning? Or should we, to fight capitalism, start an underground fight club egged on by an imaginary Brad Pitt? Are we just swimming in Postman’s “sea of irrelevance”?None of this is to suggest that an Instagram challenge dictates all our choices or is a sign of a silent totalitarianism.But the algorithm and our non-stop access to the internet, coupled with generative AI, mean that we are jacked in all the time.The algorithm watches us linger and knows exactly what to serve next. The longer we linger, the more it knows. Perhaps that also explains why the modern internet is so obsessed with the self. Narcissus had to make do with a pool. We have better tech and a metaphorical pool that can make us look younger, thinner, richer, more muscular, better dressed or like an anime character.The mirror reflected our own image, social media taught us to become performative and market the self, and now AI allows us to manufacture alternative selves before deciding which one to show to the world.There’s nothing profoundly new about vanity. Pharaohs got slaves to build pyramids, aristocrats commissioned portraits and people with existential angst learnt to put their ontological problems on paper to become writers.Now we have one giant machine that will do all of it for us: make us look better and even write our essays about existential angst. But a true writer knows that whatever is written by a machine is never truly human and is, at best, a pale imitation drawn from patterns in previous works.In The Matrix, you freed yourself by realising that you were in a dream world. And in the real world, you do it with the book bait that I promised in the starting of the Vine. Most folks consider Nineteen Eighty-Four and Brave New World the two magnum opuses of dystopian novels but I believe there’s a third book that deserves to be on the same pedestal: Fahrenheit 451 by Ray Bradbury whose plot has the key to saving humanity.In this dystopia, books are banned and firefighters’ job is to burn them, not save people from fires. And that’s what we need to rediscover because, since the Gutenberg press came around, books became far more commonplace than it used to be no longer preserve of the elite. Almost everyone could learn to read and write. That ability expanded with the internet democratising information unlike any previous explosion in human history. Today we have machines in our pockets that are vastly more powerful than the computers that helped send man to the Moon, and we use them to argue with strangers and generate AI slop.Why not use them to rediscover what made us human?The answer is embarrassingly simple: read more, scroll less and occasionally allow your mind to belong entirely to you. We don’t have to live in Orwell’s or Huxley’s world. Bradbury feared a world where books had to be burnt; ours might be worse if we simply stop wanting to read them.In The Matrix, you freed yourself by realising that you were in a dream world. And in the real world, you do it with the book bait that I promised at the start of the Vine. We don’t have to live in Orwell’s or Huxley’s world. Bradbury feared a world where books had to be burnt; ours might be worse if we simply stop wanting to read them.So forget the ’80s challenge. If you really want to revisit the past, try the radical old habit of picking up a book.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: In 1914, a Connecticut writer opened one of America’s first private songbird sanctuaries; her work helped shape a statewide bird-protection movement that still operates
articles.summary: Explore the rich history of Birdcraft Sanctuary in Connecticut, established in 1914 by conservationist Mabel Osgood Wright, and its ongoing impact on bird protection and conservation efforts in the state.
articles.body: Birdcraft Sanctuary was founded in Fairfield, Connecticut, in 1914, and the Connecticut Audubon Society describes it as one of the first private songbird sanctuaries in the United States. It is a National Historic Landmark. Its creator was Mabel Osgood Wright, a writer and conservationist who had already spent years pressing for laws to protect birds. The sanctuary did not start the state's bird-protection effort so much as give it a home. Wright helped found the Connecticut Audubon Society in 1898, sixteen years earlier, and the society still operates. Its history page lists centers and sanctuaries across the state, along with an advocacy program in Hartford that has run since 1974.Wright helped found the Connecticut Audubon Society in January 1898The Connecticut Audubon Society's history page says a small group of women in Fairfield founded it in 1898, including Wright, Helen Glover, Theodora Wheeler and Harriet Glover. A profile of Wright, written by a later chair of the society's board and republished in 2023, puts the founding in January 1898 and says Wright served as president until 1924. Wright was also a prolific author. The profile counts 27 books, beginning with The Friendship of Nature in 1894. Her 1895 bird guide, Birdcraft, was reprinted nine times and served as the most popular bird guide until Roger Tory Peterson’s Field Guide to the Birds appeared in 1934. She joined the founding board of the National Association of Audubon Societies in 1905, though the Connecticut society stayed independent when that group became the National Audubon Society in 1940.Annie Burr Jennings funded a 10-acre former pasture that opened as Birdcraft in 1914Wright had earlier advocated for "songbird reservations" before she made one. After she and some friends watched a play about a feather hunter who became a bird conservationist, Jennings urged that Connecticut needed a sanctuary and that Wright should create it. Jennings's gift of 10 acres in 1914, the society's history page says, let Wright create Birdcraft Sanctuary. The land was a piece of former pasture within walking distance from the train station and near the Wright residence. It contained trees and berry bushes which were favorable for the birds. Workers erected a fence designed to keep away cats, created paths, planted shrubbery, constructed a cabin for a caretaker, and dredged a pond fed by springs. Wright planned the sanctuary as both a refuge for birds and a place where people could observe them.Nearly 1,000 visitors in the first month drove the birds away and led to a museumThe public reaction almost ruined the whole plan. According to the profile of Wright, nearly 1,000 visitors came in the first month, and the birds vanished. Instead of limiting access, however, the board came up with a different idea. Visitors would keep bringing dead birds and asking about them, so the caretaker, Frank Novak, who was also a taxidermist, would mount them. This resulted in the creation of a one-room museum with seasonal displays, this time funded by Jennings, the construction of which began in late November 1914 and which opened in March 1915. By July 1, 1915, the sanctuary had received 1,300 visitors, and 52 nests were recorded in its first year. It also followed the harsher management practices of its era: cats were not allowed, and predatory birds were removed as well.Bird-protection bills from 1907 to 1919 came out of the society Wright ledHer efforts transcended the fence line. According to the profile, the society she helped form backed legislation on hunting control in 1907, protection of birds and eggs from collectors in 1911, sandpipers in 1912 and the International Migratory Bird Treaty Act in 1918. It opposed a bounty on Bald Eagles in 1919. Once the bills were approved, Wright campaigned for their enforcement. Frank Chapman described Birdcraft in Bird-Lore as "an object lesson in conservation and museum methods." Birdcraft became a model for other projects. Bird-Craft also inspired the Theodore Roosevelt Memorial Sanctuary in Oyster Bay, after Roosevelt's widow visited while seeking a fitting memorial.The 1957 Interstate 95 route took nearly half the land, and landmark status came in 1993After Wright died in 1934, the sanctuary changed drastically. According to the Connecticut Audubon Society's profile of Wright, the construction of Interstate 95 in 1957 took nearly half of Birdcraft Sanctuary's land. The state initially offered $20,000 in compensation, and appeals failed because it did not recognize the property's value as a sanctuary. The final settlement was $42,000, which the profile says fell far short of covering the loss.However, even then, the place continued serving its purpose. Even so, the sanctuary kept serving its purpose: migrating birds still use the pond and dense vegetation between the highway and the railroad. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1993. According to the society's Birdcraft web page, more than 150 bird species have been recorded there, and it is a federally licensed bird banding station.The society now operates sanctuaries and a Hartford advocacy programAccording to its history page, the society opened the Center at Fairfield in 1971, the Coastal Center at Milford Point in 1995 and the Center at Pomfret in 2000, and it launched its Science in Nature program in 2012. Since 1974, its Hartford advocacy program has contributed to every major environmental initiative in Connecticut. This information makes a cautious interpretation of the legacy of the sanctuary justified. Birdcraft did not found the bird protection campaign in Connecticut, as it was established by the society back in 1898. However, it provided this campaign with its public location, a way of teaching people about birds, and a record of success, and it continues to work as an organization.You use AI every day.
