articles.title: $26,000 to fight for Russia: How Moscow recruits Americans via TikTok and Telegram
articles.summary: Russia is increasingly turning to foreign recruits to replenish its forces fighting in Ukraine, with at least 18 Americans identified as having joined the
articles.body: Russia is increasingly turning to foreign recruits to replenish its forces fighting in Ukraine, with at least 18 Americans identified as having joined the Russian military, according to Ukrainian officials cited by the New York Post. US recruits are reportedly being offered a signing bonus of about $26,000, along with a monthly salary.The recruitment is being driven through a network of agents who use platforms including Facebook, TikTok and Telegram to find potential recruits. Ukrainian officials said recruiters can earn money for each person they bring in, with some reportedly receiving about $24,000 per recruit as well as a share of the recruit’s salary.The effort extends far beyond Americans. Ukrainian security officials have identified nearly 29,000 foreigners from 135 countries fighting for Russia, although the actual number could be higher. Amnesty International has separately documented deceptive and exploitative recruitment practices targeting foreign nationals, including promises of civilian jobs, high salaries, legal status or Russian citizenship.US citizens joining Russia's warOne of those recruited was Seth William Baker, a former US Marine from Gilbert, Arizona. Baker, who had served as a lance corporal and worked as a bulk fuel specialist, was 23 when he was killed on the frontlines in Ukraine, around three months after signing up.Baker had joined the Marines at 18 but was later discharged after refusing the military's Covid-19 vaccine mandate. He subsequently became involved with Russian propaganda online before travelling to Russia.In a recording made from a Russian bunker, Baker said the vaccine mandate had been one of the factors behind his decision to leave the US military and join Russia's war effort.Vitaliy Matvienko, who heads Ukraine's state-backed project encouraging Russian soldiers to surrender, described Baker's case as typical of the people Russia's recruitment network seeks out. He said Russia had turned foreign recruitment into an “entire industry” as it struggles to replace battlefield losses.Baker is not the only American identified as having fought for Russia.Michael Gloss, 21, the son of a former CIA official, was killed while fighting in Ukraine in April 2024. Ukrainian intelligence has also identified 17 other Americans who had enlisted in the Russian military.Another case involves former Massachusetts city councillor Wilmer Puello-Mota, who left the US while facing a child sexual-abuse-related case and later joined Russian forces. He was wounded by shrapnel in Ukraine in August.Derek Huffman, 47, moved his family to Russia and later signed up for the military, according to the report. He had previously criticised what he described as LGBTQ “indoctrination” in the US and said he wanted to earn respect and Russian citizenship.Matvienko said foreign recruits serve a dual purpose for Moscow: they provide additional manpower while also allowing Russia to portray Americans and other foreigners fighting alongside its troops as evidence of international support for its war.Foreign recruits can also be easier for Russia to absorb politically when they are killed, he said, because their deaths do not necessarily generate the same reaction inside Russian society as the deaths of Russian soldiers.The recruitment comes as Russia continues to sustain heavy battlefield losses. Ukrainian officials cited by the New York Post estimated that Russia was suffering tens of thousands of casualties each month and increasingly relying on foreign nationals to help fill its ranks.You use AI every day. articles.title: Minnesota has picked a nearly 57-acre site for a $1 billion horticulture world's fair expected to draw millions; after the six-month Expo ends, the land is planned to become a permanent mixed-use district
articles.summary: Minnesota has selected Lakeville as the planned host city for Expo 2031, a six-month international exhibition focused on horticulture.
articles.body: Minnesota has selected Lakeville as the planned host city for Expo 2031, a six-month international exhibition focused on horticulture. According to Minnesota Star Tribune, organisers have signed a purchase agreement for nearly 57 acres of land near Interstate 35 and County Road 70, with the event expected to attract millions of visitors.The Expo is scheduled to run from May to October 2031. It would be the first A1 International Horticultural Exhibition to be held in the United States. These exhibitions bring together international pavilions, gardens and programmes focused on horticulture and related themes.The event is being planned on a much larger scale than the 57-acre parcel already secured. Wendy Meadley, CEO and board chair of Expo 2031, said the remaining land needed for the project would be acquired through methods including leasing. The total area involved is expected to be about 180 acres.Expo around horticulture and 'Human/Nature'Expo 2031 is being planned around the theme “Human/Nature”. The exhibition is expected to include international and national pavilions, gardens and other visitor attractions.Plans for the Lakeville site currently include a 200-room hotel, a 1,300-space parking structure, an Expo Hall and a community welcome centre. The site is also planned to have a media studio and a 1,500-person amphitheatre.Another proposed feature is a “secret garden” that could also be used as a wedding venue. The plans include a USA Pavilion with what organisers described as “Bellagio-style” fountains.Meadley told KARE 11 that organisers are planning for between 4 million and 6 million visitors during the six-month event. The organisers have said the event would bring millions of people to the southern suburbs and increase activity for local businesses.“We have a project that has moved from vision to development,” Meadley said during a presentation to the Lakeville City Council on September 21.The site is currently vacant land. It is owned by the United Christian Academy Foundation, which has agreed to sell the nearly 57-acre parcel to Expo 2031, according to the Minnesota Star Tribune.Organisers expect development to continue The plans for Expo 2031 go beyond the six-month exhibition. Organisers want parts of the development to remain after the event and become a longer-term site.The planned USA Pavilion is a major part of that approach. Meadley said the project needed a substantial legacy feature that would continue to exist after the Expo rather than being built only for the event. “It’s about a billion-dollar project,” Meadley told the Lakeville City Council.The current budget is just under $1 billion, according to the Minnesota Star Tribune. KARE 11 reported that the figure is more than twice the estimate given when Dakota County was pitching to host the event in 2024.Meadley said the higher figure includes the economics around the USA Pavilion, which organisers consider the project's main legacy feature. “If you look at the Eiffel Tower or the Seattle Needle (other World's Fair legacy projects) what we believed was a tower or an edifice of that type wasn’t enough,” Meadley said. “We believe there had to be something much more robust that would live on in the future.”Lakeville residents question projectThe proposed Expo has also brought questions from people living and working near the site, particularly about its cost, traffic and whether the project will be completed.Dan Mullin, who owns an auto repair shop across a gravel road from the undeveloped land, said he had heard rumours about the Expo for months before the plans were confirmed.Mullin said he was encouraged by the renderings showing how the site could be transformed. However, he remains cautious because he has seen previous plans for the land that did not move ahead.“A couple of times a summer, it seems like there’s a whole group of people that are up there doing those (photos) where they’re all taking a scoop of dirt and throwing it and then nothing happens,” Mullin said. “I think it’s fifty-fifty that they’re gonna be able to pull it off.” He also questioned the project’s price and timeline.Traffic and public outreachWith millions of visitors expected over six months, managing traffic and the effect on daily life in Lakeville is another part of the planning.Meadley said organisers want visitors to arrive steadily throughout the six-month Expo rather than creating concentrated pressure on local infrastructure. Shuttle buses and other measures are being considered to help manage congestion.“We know that if people can’t move around regular and have regular everyday life during those six months of expo, we’re going to have really displeased residents of the greater metro area,” she said.Mullin said he still has questions about the project but is willing to hear more about the plans. “We don’t really know if it’s good or bad yet, I feel like it probably would be good for us,” he said.Lakeville is planning public open houses with Expo organisers so residents can ask questions about the project. The first is scheduled at City Hall on October 21 from 4pm to 7pm.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
